issues.legal_issue: A tenant company’s continued possession of agricultural land after expiry of its lease remains juridical possession where the governing land-reform law provides that expiry alone does not terminate the tenancy, making the company subject to the prohibition on holding land.
material_facts: A registered company leased agricultural land for a fixed term, and the term expired.
The company remained in possession after the lease expired; the landowners were not in possession of the land at the relevant time.
The land-reform law provided that a tenancy could not be terminated merely because its fixed duration had expired.
issues.conclusion: The company’s possession remained juridical despite expiry of the lease. It was required to declare the land it held, and the land covered by the declaration vested in the State free from encumbrances.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 5 and 6 of the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, a tenancy cannot be terminated merely by expiry of its fixed term. Read with Sections 19, 20, 44, 58, 60, 62 and 79-B, the Act allows only a person in possession and personally cultivating land to hold it, while prohibiting a company from holding agricultural land and requiring a company holding land to declare it. The Court distinguished Bhawanji Lakhamshi v. Himatlal Jamnadas Dani, which concerned whether landlord consent created a tenancy after expiry, and M.C. Chockalingam v. V. Manickavasagam, which concerned lawful possession under cinema licensing rules; neither displaced the effect of the statutory continuation of tenancy here.

predicates.company_landholding_restriction_case: The proceeding concerns whether a company holding agricultural land is subject to a statutory restriction on holding it.
predicates.agricultural_land_leased_to_company: An owner leased agricultural land to a company.
predicates.lease_expired_by_time: The fixed term of the lease ended.
predicates.company_remained_in_possession: The company continued to possess the land after the lease term ended.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns a company’s restricted holding of agricultural land leased to it, and the company remains in possession after the lease term ends, the company must declare the land and the land vests in the State.

issues.legal_issue: A declaration that identifies the wrong statutory provision does not deprive the competent authorities of jurisdiction to inquire into the company’s landholding and declare the land vested in the State.
material_facts: The company remained in possession of agricultural land after expiry of its lease.
The company submitted a declaration concerning the land but cited a provision governing a different declaration.

The Tehsildar conducted an inquiry and gave the landowners an opportunity to participate before submitting the matter to the Deputy Commissioner, who published the vesting declaration in the prescribed manner.
issues.conclusion: The mistaken citation did not invalidate the authorities’ jurisdiction; the inquiry and vesting declaration were valid.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 79-B(2) and 79-B(3) require a company holding land to submit a declaration and provide for an inquiry and a vesting declaration by the competent authorities. A declaration made under the wrong statutory citation may nevertheless be treated according to its substance, and the mistaken quotation does not remove the authorities’ jurisdiction to act under the applicable provision.
